citations.quote:
Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $U$.

For an open set $V \subseteq X$, define
$$(j_!\mathcal F)(V) := \left\{ s\in \mathcal F(V\cap U): \operatorname{Supp}(s)\text{ is closed in }V \right\}.$$
Equivalently, $s$ lies in $(j_!\mathcal F)(V)$ exactly when for every
$x\in V\setminus U$ there exists an open neighbourhood $W_x \subseteq V$ with
$$
s|_{W_x\cap U}=0.
$$

Restriction maps are inherited from $\mathcal F$, so $j_!\mathcal F$ is a
subsheaf of $j_*\mathcal F$. When $V \subseteq U$, the support condition is
vacuous and
$$
(j_!\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V).
$$

This is the **extension by zero** of $\mathcal F$ along $j$. It is distinct in
general from the ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on $X$.
The **direct image presheaf**
$$f_*\mathcal F$$
on $Y$ is defined on an open set $V \subseteq Y$ by
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V):=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V)).
$$
If $V' \subseteq V$, the restriction map
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V)\longrightarrow(f_*\mathcal F)(V')
$$
is the restriction map of $\mathcal F$ for the inclusion
$f^{-1}(V') \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.

Thus direct image is just precomposition of the presheaf with the inverse-image
map on open sets.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map.

1. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $X$, then $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $Y$.
2. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of groups, rings, or modules on $X$, then
   $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of the same kind on $Y$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). This is a subgroup: the zero section has empty support, negation preserves
support, and the support of a sum is closed in $X$ and contained in the finite
union of the two compact supports, hence compact
([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]],
[[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).
A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be abelian categories, let $I$ be supplied
injective resolution data on all objects of $\mathcal A$, and let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor. Then the additive functors
$$R_I^nF:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B,\qquad n\geq 0,$$
admit connecting maps that make them into a cohomological delta functor on
$\mathcal A$, and $R_I^0F$ is naturally isomorphic to $F$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]) and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on
$X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); this covers in particular every sheaf
of $k$-vector spaces over a field $k$, which is the case used by the
compact-support calculus, and for such a sheaf the groups below are $k$-vector
spaces and the maps $k$-linear. Global sections are written
$\Gamma(X,-)$ ([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]). For a compact subset
$K\subseteq X$ ([[def-compact-space]]) let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion and consider the canonical restriction map
$$\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K),\qquad s\longmapsto s|_K,$$
which sends a global section ([[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]) to
the section of the inverse image sheaf ([[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]])
that it induces on $K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is **c-soft**, also **soft for
compact supports**, when this map is surjective for every compact subset
$K\subseteq X$, that is: every section of $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset of
$X$ extends to a global section of $\mathcal F$. For sheaves of abelian groups
$\Gamma_c$ and $H^q_c$ of
[[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]] are the compactly supported
analogues of $\Gamma$ and $H^q$.

Two consistency facts hold; both are immediate from the definitions and from
the extension lemma for sections on a compact set, and they are recorded here
because the compact-support calculus uses the first constantly and the second
for injective sheaves.

1. **Neighbourhood formulation.** By
   [[lem-sections-near-a-compact-set-are-sections-on-that-set]], the target of
   the restriction map is the defining colimit of the
   inverse-image presheaf,
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)=\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K}\mathcal F(U)$, so that
   $\mathcal F$ is c-soft if and only if for every compact $K$ and every open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, every section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ agrees with a
   global section of $\mathcal F$ on some open neighbourhood of $K$. It
   therefore suffices, for c-softness, to test the extended sections only
   locally near $K$.
2. **Flasque implies c-soft.** If $\mathcal F$ is flasque
   ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) then $\mathcal F$ is c-soft: a class in
   $(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$ is represented by a section $s$ over an open
   neighbourhood $U$ of $K$, and flasqueness extends $s$ to a global section
   $t\in\mathcal F(X)$ with $t|_U=s$, so $t$ is a preimage of that class.

C-softness is a property of the pair $(X,\mathcal F)$ and not of the sheaf
alone: the compact subsets of the base space are part of the test. Nothing is
assumed about the support of the extended global sections, and c-softness is
not the same condition as flasqueness, only implied by it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and the tensor clause of (4) is stated only
there. Then:

1. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]), every section of
   $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a compactly
   supported global section whose support is contained in any prescribed open
   neighbourhood of $K$;
2. every injective abelian sheaf on $X$ is c-soft;
3. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft, then $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>0$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]); when $X$ is compact this is
   the vanishing of the sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
4. c-softness is preserved by restriction to open subsets, by restriction to
   closed subsets, by extension by zero along an open inclusion, and by finite
   direct sums of sheaves of abelian groups; for sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
   it is also preserved by tensor product with a constant $k$-vector space;
5. if $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal F''\to0$
   is a short exact sequence of sheaves of abelian groups and $\mathcal F'$ is
   c-soft, then every section of $\mathcal F''$ over a compact subset lifts to
   a section of $\mathcal F$ over an open neighbourhood of it, and the induced
   sequence
   $0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')\to0$
   is exact; if $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal F$ are c-soft then
   $\mathcal F''$ is c-soft.

Let $X$ be a topological space, let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf of $k$-vector
spaces (or of abelian groups) on $X$
([[def-presheaf-on-topological-space]]), let $U\subseteq X$ be open and let
$s\in\mathcal F(U)$. The **support of $s$** is
$$\operatorname{Supp}(s):=\{\,x\in U: s_x\neq 0\,\}\subseteq U,$$
where $s_x\in\mathcal F_x$ denotes the germ of $s$ at $x$ in the stalk
$\mathcal F_x$ ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]], [[def-germ-of-section]]). A section
$s\in\mathcal F(X)$ is **compactly supported** when its support is a compact
subspace of $X$ ([[def-compact-space]]). For a subspace $Z\subseteq X$ and a
presheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Z$, the support of $t\in\mathcal G(Z)$ is defined by
the same condition using the stalks of $\mathcal G$. The support is not assumed
closed in $X$ nor compact.

When $\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** of abelian groups (in particular of $k$-vector spaces) the following three
consistency facts hold; they are immediate consequences of the definitions
above and are recorded here because every later compact-support statement uses
them.

1. $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is closed in $U$. Indeed, if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk; equality of germs means
   that $s$ and the zero section agree on some open neighbourhood $W\subseteq U$
   of $x$ ([[def-germ-of-section]]), so $s$ vanishes on the open neighbourhood
   $W$ of $x$, and $U\setminus\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is therefore open in $U$.
2. $\operatorname{Supp}(s)=\varnothing$ if and only if $s=0$. If every germ of
   $s$ is zero then $s=0$ by the locality axiom of a sheaf applied to the cover
   of $U$ by its open subsets ([[lem-section-zero-if-all-germs-zero]]); the
   converse is immediate, since the zero section has zero germ at every point.
3. $\operatorname{Supp}(s|_V)=\operatorname{Supp}(s)\cap V$ for every open
   $V\subseteq U$. Restriction is compatible with the germ maps, so
   $(s|_V)_x=s_x$ for every $x\in V$ ([[def-germ-of-section]]).

For a sheaf, a section whose support is contained in a compact subset
$C\subseteq U$ is compactly supported: its support is closed in $C$ by fact 1,
hence compact ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).
For a global section ($U=X$), this applies to any compact subset of $X$.
For a local section, containment in a compact subset of $X$ alone does not
suffice: the constant nonzero section of the constant sheaf
([[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]])
on $U=(0,1)\subseteq X=[0,1]$ has
support $U$, which is not compact although it is contained in the compact $X$
([[cor-heine-borel-in-the-product-topology]], $n=1$).
The open cover $\{(1/n,1):n\ge2\}$ of $U$ has no finite subcover.
No choice principle is used: germs, stalks, supports and restrictions are elementary.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). Then:

1. **A neighbourhood base of compact sets.** If $X$ is locally compact
   ([[def-locally-compact-space]]) and Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]), then
   every neighbourhood $N$ of a point $x \in X$ ([[def-neighbourhood-top]])
   contains a compact neighbourhood of $x$; so the compact neighbourhoods of $x$
   form a neighbourhood base at $x$.
2. **Heredity along open and closed subspaces.** If $X$ is locally compact and
   Hausdorff and $S \subseteq X$ is open, then the subspace $S$ is locally
   compact ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). If $X$ is locally compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed, then the subspace $F$ is locally compact; no
   Hausdorff hypothesis is used for this half.
3. **Shrinking inside an open set.** If $X$ is locally compact and Hausdorff,
   $O \subseteq X$ is open and $x \in O$, there is an open $V$ with
   $$x \in V \subseteq \overline{V} \subseteq O$$
   and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of $X$.
4. **Compact sets sit in open sets with compact closure.** If $X$ is locally
   compact and Hausdorff and $K \subseteq X$ is compact, there is an open
   $V \subseteq X$ with $K \subseteq V$ and $\overline{V}$ a compact subset of
   $X$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-top]]).

**No choice principle is used**; every cover produced below is defined by a
formula and thinned by [[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]], which returns
members rather than indices.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let
$A \subseteq X$ and let $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ be the subspace
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **Compactness read in the ambient space.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$
   ([[def-compact-space]]), that is $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact space, if
   and only if for every family $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ with
   $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n$,
   or else $A = \varnothing$.
2. **The same in indexed form.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$ if and only if
   for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$
   with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   indices $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with
   $A \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $A = \varnothing$.

Claim 2 is the form used by almost every later proof on this page, because a
cover is usually produced by a rule that attaches an open set to each point or to
each index, and a set of open sets forgets that rule. No choice principle is used
anywhere below; the one place a selection is made is over a finite index set, and
[[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.
The properties $T_0$, $T_1$, and Hausdorffness are hereditary in the sense of [[def-hereditary-property]].

Let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of sets on a topological space $X$. Then
$\mathcal F(\varnothing)$ is a singleton.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, and let $X$ be a topological space. Then
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ has enough injectives, every abelian sheaf on $X$ admits an
injective resolution ([[def-injective-resolution-in-an-abelian-category]]), and
the embeddings below supply one injective resolution datum
([[def-supplied-injective-resolution-datum]]) on the whole category
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)$: for every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ the datum assigns one
specific injective resolution
$$0\to\mathcal F\to I^0(\mathcal F)\to I^1(\mathcal F)\to\cdots,$$
built functorially from $\mathcal F$ with no further selection.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$ in an
abelian category. For every morphism $u:A\to B$ with $A,B\in\mathcal D$, there
exists a coaugmentation-preserving cochain map
$$\widetilde u^\bullet:I^\bullet(A)\to I^\bullet(B)$$
extending $u$.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor, and let
$$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to J^2\to\cdots$$
be an $F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$. Assume moreover that
$A\in\mathcal D$ and that, for $Z^0:=A$ and
$$0\to Z^q\to J^q\to Z^{q+1}\to0\qquad(q\ge0),$$
each $Z^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ there is a canonical
isomorphism
$$R_I^nF(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(F(J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}})).$$

Let $F$ be an additive functor between abelian categories.

1. If $F$ is left exact and $I$ is a supplied injective resolution datum on a
   class $\mathcal D$, an **$F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$** is
   a coaugmented exact complex
   $$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to\cdots$$
   such that every $J^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$ and is $F$-acyclic in the sense
   of
   [[def-acyclic-object-for-a-left-exact-functor]].
2. If $F$ is right exact and $P$ is a supplied projective resolution datum on a
   class $\mathcal D$, an **$F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $P$** is
   an augmented exact complex
   $$\cdots\to P_1\to P_0\to A\to0$$
   such that every $P_q$ lies in $\mathcal D$ and is $F$-acyclic in the sense
   of
   [[def-acyclic-object-for-a-right-exact-functor]].

Thus the phrase keeps both the resolution orientation and the chosen supplied
datum visible.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, and
let $F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor between
abelian categories.

An object $A\in\mathcal D$ is **$F$-acyclic** if
$$R_I^nF(A)=0\qquad\text{for every }n>0.$$

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on the same domain and
one assumes the Axiom of Dependent Choice, then
[[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]
gives natural isomorphisms $R_I^nF(A)\cong R_J^nF(A)$ for every $n$. Under
that additional hypothesis, this vanishing condition is independent of the
chosen supplied injective datum.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum, let
$F,G:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be additive functors, and let
$\alpha:F\Rightarrow G$ be a natural transformation. Then for every
$n\in\mathbb Z$ the maps
$$\mathbf R_I^n(\alpha)_A:=H^n\!\bigl(\alpha_{I(A)_{\mathrm{del}}}\bigr):R_I^nF(A)\to R_I^nG(A)$$
define a natural transformation
$$\mathbf R_I^n(\alpha):R_I^nF\Rightarrow R_I^nG.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $K\subseteq X$ be a compact subset ([[def-compact-space]]) of a locally
compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-hausdorff-space]]),
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let $i:K\hookrightarrow X$ be the
inclusion. Then the canonical map
$$\varinjlim_{U\supseteq K,\ U\ \text{open}}\mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow\Gamma(K,i^{-1}\mathcal F)=(i^{-1}\mathcal F)(K)$$
is an isomorphism of abelian groups (of $k$-vector spaces when $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces). Moreover, for pairwise disjoint compact
subsets $K_1,\dots,K_m\subseteq X$ and sections $s_j\in\mathcal F(U_j)$ over open
neighbourhoods $U_j$ of the respective $K_j$, there are an open neighbourhood $U$
of $K_1\cup\dots\cup K_m$ and a section $s\in\mathcal F(U)$, together with, for
every $j$, an open neighbourhood $W_j\subseteq U_j$ of $K_j$ with
$s|_{W_j}=s_j|_{W_j}$; in particular the zero section can be prescribed on any
compact set disjoint from the given one. The isomorphism is $k$-linear in the vector-space case, and no
choice principle is used: every selection in the proof is made from finitely
many nonempty sets.

derivations.claim: **Clause (1), degree zero.** By [F1], $(j_!\mathcal A)(X)=\{\,s\in\mathcal A(U):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{closed in }X\,\}$. For such $s$ the support of $s$ read as a global section of $j_!\mathcal A$ is the same set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)\subseteq U$: at $x\in U$ the stalks of $j_!\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal A$ agree with compatible germ identifications, while for $x\notin U$ the germ of $s$ vanishes, because the defining local condition supplies an open neighbourhood $W_x$ with $s|_{W_x\cap U}=0$, so the restriction of $s$ to $W_x$ is already the zero element of $(j_!\mathcal A)(W_x)$. Hence, using that compactness of a subset of $U$ may be read in $U$ or in $X$ and that compact subsets of $X$ are closed [F6], the subgroups $\Gamma_c(X,j_!\mathcal A)=\{\,s\in(j_!\mathcal A)(X):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{compact in }X\,\}$ and $\{\,s\in\mathcal A(U):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{compact in }U\,\}=\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal A)$ are equal inside $\mathcal A(U)$; the canonical map is the inclusion of these equal subgroups, hence a bijection, and it is natural in $\mathcal A$ because $j_!\varphi$ acts as $\varphi$ on sections of $\mathcal A(U)$.

**Clause (2), degree zero and stalks of $i_*$.** By [F2], $(i_*\mathcal B)(X)=\mathcal B(X\cap Z)=\mathcal B(Z)$. The stalks are computed as follows: for $z\in Z$ the sets $V\cap Z$ with $V$ an open neighbourhood of $z$ in $X$ are exactly the open neighbourhoods of $z$ in $Z$ and are cofinal in the colimit defining the stalk, and $(i_*\mathcal B)(V)=\mathcal B(V\cap Z)$ for each of them, so the two colimit diagrams agree and $(i_*\mathcal B)_z\cong\mathcal B_z$; for $x\notin Z$ the open set $X\setminus Z=U$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ with $(i_*\mathcal B)(W)=\mathcal B(W\cap Z)=\mathcal B(\varnothing)=0$ for every open $W\subseteq U$, so $(i_*\mathcal B)_x=0$. Consequently for $t\in\mathcal B(Z)$ the support of $t$ read as a global section of $i_*\mathcal B$ is the set $\operatorname{Supp}(t)\subseteq Z$, and compactness of a subset of $Z$ may be read in $Z$ or in $X$ [F6]; hence $\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)=\{\,t\in\mathcal B(Z):\operatorname{Supp}(t)\ \text{compact in }Z\,\}=\Gamma_c(Z,\mathcal B)$, the canonical map is the identity, and it is natural in $\mathcal B$ because $i_*\varphi$ acts as $\varphi$ on sections over $Z$.

**Clause (1), c-softness.** Let $\mathcal A$ be c-soft on $U$, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and represent a section over $K$ by $s\in(j_!\mathcal A)(V)$ for $V\supseteq K$ open [F10]. Its support is closed in $V$, so $L:=K\cap\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ is compact and contained in $V\cap U$ [F1, F5, F6]. If $L=\varnothing$, the zero global section has the same germs on $K$. Otherwise choose opens $W_0,W_1$ with $L\subseteq W_0\subseteq\overline{W_0}\subseteq W_1\subseteq\overline{W_1}\subseteq V\cap U$ and compact closures [F6]. The sets $T:=K\cap\overline{W_1}$ and $C:=\overline{W_1}\setminus W_0$ are compact in $U$. The class of $s$ on $T$ and the zero class on $C$ agree on $T\cap C$, since its points lie in $K\setminus L$ and have zero germ of $s$. Fuse these classes near their union in $U$ [F10], and use c-softness of $\mathcal A$ to extend the resulting class to $g\in\Gamma(U,\mathcal A)$, with $g=s$ near $T$ and $g=0$ near $C$ [F4, F10]. Glue $g|_{W_1}$ with zero on $U\setminus\overline{W_0}$, since the overlap lies in $C$. The result $e$ has support closed in $U$ and contained in compact $\overline{W_0}\subseteq U$, hence $e\in\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal A)=\Gamma_c(X,j_!\mathcal A)$ by step 1.1. On $K\cap W_1$ its germs are those of $s$; on $K\setminus\overline{W_0}$ both vanish, because $L\subseteq W_0$. These sets cover $K$, so $e$ restricts to the original section over $K$. Hence $j_!\mathcal A$ is c-soft.

**$i_*$ is exact.** Let $0\to\mathcal B'\to\mathcal B\to\mathcal B''\to0$ be an exact sequence of sheaves on $Z$ and apply $i_*$ degreewise; by [F7] it suffices to test exactness of the resulting sequence at every stalk of $X$. At a point $z\in Z$ the stalk sequence of the $i_*$-images is the given exact stalk sequence under the identifications $(i_*\mathcal B)_z\cong\mathcal B_z$ of [step 1.2], and at a point $x\notin Z$ all three stalks vanish by [step 1.2], so the sequence $0\to0\to0\to0$ is exact there. Hence $i_*$ sends exact sequences to exact sequences.

**Clause (2), c-softness.** Let $\mathcal B$ be c-soft on $Z$, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact and let $\sigma$ be a section of $i_*\mathcal B$ over $K$, represented by a section $s\in(i_*\mathcal B)(V)=\mathcal B(V\cap Z)$ over an open $V\supseteq K$ [F4]. Then $L:=K\cap Z$ is compact in $Z$ [F6] and $V\cap Z$ is an open neighbourhood of $L$ in $Z$, so c-softness of $\mathcal B$ provides $t\in\Gamma(Z,\mathcal B)$ agreeing with $s$ on an open neighbourhood $N\subseteq V\cap Z$ of $L$ [F4]. Choose open $W\subseteq X$ with $W\cap Z=N$ [F6]; the global section $t\in\mathcal B(Z)=(i_*\mathcal B)(X)$ agrees with the class $\sigma$ over $K$: at $z\in L$ the open set $W\cap V$ contains $z$ and $t|_{W\cap V}=s|_{W\cap V}$ as elements of $\mathcal B((W\cap V)\cap Z)$ because $(W\cap V)\cap Z\subseteq N$, so the germs agree, and at $x\in K\setminus Z$ the stalk $(i_*\mathcal B)_x$ vanishes by [step 1.2], so all germs there are equal. Hence $i_*\mathcal B$ is c-soft.

**Clause (1), computing both derived functors by the same complex.** Let $0\to\mathcal A\to J^0\to J^1\to\cdots$ be the injective resolution of $\mathcal A$ supplied by the fixed functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(U)$ [F7, F8]; each $J^q$ is injective, hence c-soft on the locally compact Hausdorff space $U$ [F4], hence $j_!J^q$ is c-soft on $X$ by [step 2.1], and c-soft sheaves on $X$ are acyclic for $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ [F4]. Since $j_!$ is exact [F1], the complex $0\to j_!\mathcal A\to j_!J^0\to j_!J^1\to\cdots$ is a $\Gamma_c(X,-)$-acyclic resolution of the sheaf $j_!\mathcal A$ on $X$, and the acyclic-resolution theorem gives canonical isomorphisms $R^q\Gamma_c(X,j_!\mathcal A)\cong H^q(\Gamma_c(X,j_!J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}}))$ for all $q\ge0$. For the functor $L:=\Gamma_c(X,j_!(-))$ on $\mathrm{Ab}(U)$, whose derived functors are formed with the same datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(U)$, the resolution $J^\bullet$ is likewise $L$-acyclic, and the derived functors $R^qL(\mathcal A)$ are computed by the very same complex $L(J^\bullet)=\Gamma_c(X,j_!J^\bullet)$; since both isomorphisms are the canonical isomorphisms of the acyclic-resolution theorem for the same resolution complex, they are compatible with comparison extensions of morphisms $\mathcal A\to\mathcal A'$ [F7, F8].

**Clause (2), the derived isomorphisms.** Let $0\to\mathcal B\to J^0\to J^1\to\cdots$ be the injective resolution of $\mathcal B$ supplied by the fixed datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(Z)$ [F7, F8]; each $J^q$ is injective, hence c-soft on $Z$, hence $i_*J^q$ is c-soft on $X$ by [step 2.3] and acyclic for $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ [F4]; since $i_*$ is exact by [step 2.2], the complex $0\to i_*\mathcal B\to i_*J^0\to i_*J^1\to\cdots$ is a $\Gamma_c(X,-)$-acyclic resolution of $i_*\mathcal B$, and the acyclic-resolution theorem combined with the degreewise identification $\Gamma_c(X,i_*J^q)\cong\Gamma_c(Z,J^q)$ of [step 1.2] gives canonical isomorphisms $R^q\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\cong H^q(\Gamma_c(X,i_*J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}}))\cong H^q(\Gamma_c(Z,J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}}))\cong R^q\Gamma_c(Z,\mathcal B)$ for all $q\ge0$, where the last isomorphism is the acyclic-resolution comparison on $Z$ applied to the same resolution, whose terms are acyclic for $\Gamma_c(Z,-)$ because they are c-soft on $Z$ [F4]; naturality in $\mathcal B$ holds because the outer isomorphisms are the canonical ones for the fixed resolution data and the middle one is a degreewise natural identification.

**Clause (1), the natural isomorphisms.** Put $G:=\Gamma_c(U,-)$ on $\mathrm{Ab}(U)$. Step 1.1 gives a natural isomorphism $\zeta:L\Rightarrow G$ of additive left exact functors. Applied degreewise to the supplied resolution $J^\bullet(\mathcal A)$, it gives an isomorphism of complexes $\Gamma_c(X,j_!J^\bullet)\cong\Gamma_c(U,J^\bullet)$. Taking cohomology gives natural isomorphisms $R^qL(\mathcal A)\cong R^qG(\mathcal A)$ by [F8]. Composing with the canonical comparison of step 3.1 yields $R^q\Gamma_c(X,j_!\mathcal A)\cong R^q\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal A)$ in every degree, naturally in $\mathcal A$.

**Clause (3).** Let $Z$ be compact. For every sheaf $\mathcal B$ on $Z$ the support of a global section is closed in $Z$ [F5], hence a closed subset of the compact space $Z$, hence compact, so every global section is compactly supported: $\Gamma_c(Z,\mathcal B)=\Gamma(Z,\mathcal B)$ and $H^q_c(Z,\mathcal B)=H^q(Z,\mathcal B)$ for all $q$ [F3]. Substituting into the isomorphisms of [step 1.2] for $q=0$ and of [step 3.2] for $q\ge1$ gives $\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\cong\Gamma(Z,\mathcal B)$ and $R^q\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\cong H^q(Z,\mathcal B)$ for all $q\ge0$.

**Conclusion.** Clause (1) is [step 1.1], [step 2.1] and [step 4.1]; clause (2) is [step 1.2], [step 2.3] and [step 3.2]; clause (3) is [step 4.2]. The Axiom of Choice is used only through the injective resolution data of [F7] and the comparison theorems of [F8], where dependent choice is required and follows from AC [F9].
